concepts.title: Triangles: Three Lines, Three Angles
concepts.section: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines
concepts.definition: A triangle is the most basic closed shape: three line segments joining three points make three sides, three vertices and three angles, and every triangle story begins with these six facts.
concepts.key_idea: Three intersecting lines lock each other into a rigid frame: the triangle is geometry's strongest small figure.
concepts.textbook_ref: gegp107.txt, A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines

concepts.title: The Angle Sum of a Triangle
concepts.definition: However a triangle is shaped, its three angles together always make a straight angle: tearing the corners of a paper triangle and joining them shows the 180 degrees, and the rule finds any missing angle.
concepts.key_idea: The 180-degree rule is the triangle's promise: two angles chosen, the third is already decided.
question_patterns: find the third angle when two angles are 60 and 70 degrees

solution_steps.explain: All three angles together make 180 degrees.
Remove the two known angles from 180 to get the third.

concepts.title: Types of Triangles by Sides and Angles
concepts.definition: Triangles come in families: by sides they are scalene, isosceles or equilateral, and by angles acute, right-angled or obtuse, so every triangle carries two names at once.
concepts.key_idea: Two labels per triangle: one from its sides, one from its biggest angle.

concepts.title: Checking Triangle Stories
concepts.definition: Angle-sum and side facts settle triangle puzzles: whether three given angles can form a triangle, which triangle has a bigger angle opposite a longer side, and what happens when a triangle is doubled in size.
concepts.key_idea: Rules answer questions: test any claimed triangle against the 180-degree promise before believing it.
